name: Marco Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead hand in the machine shop at Brennan Kitchens. We make kitchen cabinets, the boxes, doors and drawers, for builders and a few showrooms. I run the CNC router, which is a big flat bed where a computer-driven cutter cuts all the parts for a kitchen out of whole boards, and I keep an eye on the edge-bander that glues the edging on. I start at half seven, load the day's cutting jobs, and spend the day changing cutters, sorting parts onto trolleys and teaching Liam, my apprentice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a pile of boards turn into a whole kitchen by lunchtime. And I like teaching Liam, he's eighteen and reminds me of me. What wears me out is the dust and the money. I'm the best on the router and I'm on less than the fitters, and Brennan's is the only cabinet shop round here big enough to need a router man. Rosa, my girlfriend, does hair, and between us we've got about three weeks put by.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. I asked one about an error code on the router once, and it was right. I help my uncle Sal with quotes for his fitting jobs on Saturdays and he got me to try it for that. I'm not on it every day, but I'll use it if it saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's fine by me. Brennan's isn't exactly cutting edge anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, like most things. People got excited, a few things got easier, life goes on. I'd say that at the bench, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things carry on, and that's mostly good. My worries are the normal ones: the builders paying late, cheap flat-pack kitchens from abroad, energy prices. AI was never top of my list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep doing Saturdays with Uncle Sal, because that's an extra hundred and fifty most weeks. Keep teaching Liam. Maybe ask Brennan for a bit more, but he'll say the builders aren't paying him, which is true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned cheap flat-pack from abroad. How does that affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The builders who used to buy from us now buy flat-pack for the cheap houses. We get the nicer jobs, which is good, but there's fewer of them. That's the real competition, not some robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think teaching Liam matters to you so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone taught me. Old Ken, when I started at sixteen. He'd stand behind me and say nothing until I did something stupid, then say one word. That's how a trade should pass on, person to person.

S0.say: It was oversold like most things. People got excited, a few things got easier and life goes on.
S0.think: Things carry on, and that's mostly good. My real worries are builders paying late, cheap flat-pack imports and energy prices, not AI.
S0.do: Carries on at Brennan's and keeps doing Saturday fitting work with his uncle for about 150 most weeks. Keeps training his apprentice and may ask for a raise, though he expects the answer to be no.
S0.quote: He'd stand behind me and say nothing until I did something stupid, then say one word.
S0.fieldNote: Marco's worries in the calm picture are classic small-business pressures: late payments, imports and energy prices. He values the handing down of a trade, from old Ken to him and from him to Liam. The Saturday work with his uncle is already an important second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady change. Yeah, I can see that. Brennan already talks about a robot for the edge-bander.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, businesses have to keep up or they go under. If Brennan doesn't modernise, the flat-pack people will eat him alive. But I'd also say keep the apprenticeships going, because someone has to know the trade when the robot breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit uneasy. A robot could load and unload the router, and the software already does the cutting plans. What's left for me is fixing things and the tricky one-off jobs. That's still a job, but maybe only for one person, and Liam might not get his chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen one of these loading robots working at another shop, I'd tell Brennan I want to be trained on it. I'd use the AI more for the router programs, because the young lads at the supplier's training day said it saves them hours. And I'd do more Saturdays with Sal, maybe Sundays too, just to have something growing on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared. More like when the router starts making a noise you haven't heard before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Liam might not get his chance. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn everything, the router, the robot, and fitting with Sal. Have three things in your hands, not one. That's what my dad said about money, and it works for trades too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you go to see the loading robot working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a bigger kitchen firm two hours away that already has one. Their router man and me met on a training day years ago. I'd ring him and ask to come and watch for a morning. I'd trust what he says over any salesman.

S1.say: Businesses have to keep up or the flat-pack firms will eat them alive. But keep the apprenticeships going, because someone has to know the trade when the robot breaks.
S1.think: A robot could load the router and the software already plans the cuts, so what's left is fixing things and tricky one-offs. That might be a job for only one person, and Liam might lose his chance.
S1.do: Visits a bigger kitchen firm to watch a loading robot work, then asks Brennan to train him on it. Uses AI more for router programs and adds more weekend fitting work with his uncle.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an unfamiliar noise from the router.
S1.quote: Have three things in your hands, not one.
S1.fieldNote: Marco accepts modernisation as the price of a business surviving, in line with his free-market views, but insists on keeping apprenticeships. He'll only trust the new robot after seeing it at a shop he knows. His concern for his apprentice Liam is as strong as his concern for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And the robots do the hands-on stuff as well. So fitting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should pull together, families and communities, and not just wait for the government. I'd also say we need to make sure young people still have something to do, because idle hands are trouble. That's how I'd put it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. The router goes, and if robots can fit a kitchen then Sal's business goes too, and that's my backup. I'd have three weeks of money and nothing in my hands that still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa and I would cut right back, no holiday, no new car, cheapest everything. I'd take every hour Brennan and Sal would give me while there's still work, and put it all away. I'd talk to my family about pooling, maybe Rosa and me moving into my nan's spare rooms, she's been asking for company anyway. And I'd look at what's left that people want a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper worried. I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said idle hands are trouble. Are you worried about yourself, or someone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Liam, mostly. He's eighteen, he's had a bit of trouble before, and this job straightened him out. If it goes, I don't know what he does. I'd try to keep him with me, whatever I end up doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rosa think about her own work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She reckons people will always want a person doing their hair, for the chat if nothing else. She might be right. So she might end up carrying us for a while. That's hard for me to say.

S2.say: People should pull together as families and communities instead of waiting for the government. Young people still need something to do, because idle hands are trouble.
S2.think: It scares me, because the router goes and Sal's fitting business, my backup, goes too. I'd have three weeks of money and nothing in my hands that still counts.
S2.do: Cuts back hard with Rosa, takes every hour Brennan and Sal offer and saves it all. Talks with family about pooling, including moving into his grandmother's spare rooms.
S2.feel: Proper worried, lying awake running numbers.
S2.quote: I'd have three weeks of money and nothing in my hands that still counts.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI wipes out both Marco's main job and his backup at once, which is what alarms him most. His instinct is family pooling and hard work rather than public help, consistent with his traditional outlook. He found it hard to say that Rosa might carry them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get some things lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort ourselves out if we start now. Get people into trades that last, keep the young ones learning. I'd say businesses should train people, not just bin them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to see what works first and then move. That's how I do things. I'd watch the robots come into other shops and see what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get trained on the new kit at Brennan's in the first year, because that keeps the wage coming for a few years. I'd save harder, maybe a hundred a week if we're careful. I'd talk to Sal properly about the business, whether there's something in installing and servicing the new kitchen machines rather than fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I've got time to do something, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'servicing kitchen machines' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kitchens are getting smarter, ovens that talk to your phone, all that. If robots fit them, someone still has to sort the problems on site, at least for a while. Sal's got the name round here. I've got the tech side. Might work. Might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether it's working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the phone rings. Sal's always said that. If the phone stops ringing, change something. He's been fitting thirty years and never once advertised.

S3.say: There's time to sort ourselves out if we start now, by getting people into trades that last. Businesses should train people, not just bin them.
S3.think: Five years is enough to see what works first and then move, which is how I do things. I'd watch robots come into other shops and see what's left.
S3.do: Gets trained on the new equipment at Brennan's in the first year to keep his wage for a few years and saves about 100 a week. Works with his uncle on shifting the business from fitting to servicing smart kitchen equipment.
S3.feel: Anxious, but helped by having time to act.
S3.quote: If the phone stops ringing, change something.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Marco's habit of watching others first, and he'd build a bridge job plus a family business idea. He's openly unsure whether servicing smart kitchens will last. His uncle Sal's simple business rules guide much of his thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time in kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. Get trained, work hard, look after your family. And keep the apprenticeships going, because people learn best from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be all right for most of it. Ten years is enough to build something with Sal. He's sixty-one, he'll want to stop soon, and he's got no kids. I think about taking it over anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brennan's for a few years, get trained on whatever they bring in, and save. Around year three I'd buy into Sal's business, slowly, a share at a time. I'd take Liam with me if he wants. And I'd use the AI for the business side, quotes and planning, because that's where it really helps a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, way back. Mostly I'd feel like I have a fair run at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you'd move into your nan's spare rooms. With ten you'd buy into a business. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. Time is money, isn't it. With two years I'm protecting what I've got. With ten, I can actually build something. Sal started his firm with a van and a drill and fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And at the end of the ten years, when robots can fit kitchens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe the firm becomes the one that runs the robots instead of the one that gets replaced by them. Or maybe it doesn't. I'd rather own something than nothing when it comes.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so no excuses: get trained, work hard and look after your family. Keep apprenticeships going, because people learn best from people.
S4.think: I'd probably be all right for most of the decade, with time to build something with Sal. He's 61 with no kids, and I already think about taking over his firm.
S4.do: Stays at Brennan's a few years, trains on new equipment and saves, then buys into his uncle's business a share at a time from about year three. Takes Liam along if he wants and uses AI for quotes and planning.
S4.feel: A faint unease, but mostly a sense of having a fair run at it.
S4.quote: I'd rather own something than nothing when it comes.
S4.fieldNote: A decade turns Marco from protecting what he has to building something, by buying into his uncle's firm. His plan rests on family and ownership, which fits his traditional, free-market views. He's honest that he doesn't know if the firm survives once robots can fit kitchens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job and my backup with Sal would both go at once, and three weeks of money doesn't go far. What would help is keeping apprenticeships and training going, paid by the firms bringing the robots in, and a bit of help for small family businesses to change what they do. I'd rather work for it than get handed it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young lads. Everyone worries about the older ones near retirement. But Liam's eighteen, and if the trades go, he's got nothing to grow into.

headlineQuote: If the trades go, he's got nothing to grow into.
portrait: Marco is a 27-year-old lead hand on the CNC router at a kitchen cabinet maker, earning less than the fitters, with about three weeks saved with his girlfriend Rosa, a hairdresser. He works Saturdays with his uncle Sal's fitting business and is deeply attached to his apprentice Liam and to passing on a trade person to person. He accepts that businesses must modernise and adopts new kit once he's seen it work elsewhere. Fast AGI alarms him because it would take both his job and his backup, leaving family pooling as his main plan. With a decade he'd buy into Sal's business and build something of his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his factory job and his backup work with his uncle would both disappear at once.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and training paid by the firms bringing in robots, and help for small family businesses to change what they do, rather than handouts.
